issues.legal_issue: An appellate authority in a rent-control appeal may admit additional evidence when further inquiry is warranted for fair disposal and the opposing party has a fair opportunity to address it.
material_facts: The landlord sought to introduce additional evidence in an appeal from the Rent Controller’s rejection of the eviction petition.
The pleadings did not clearly set out the allegation concerning the landlord’s sale of another house.
The parties had an opportunity to test and address the additional evidence, and the Court found no prejudice to the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The appellate authority had jurisdiction to admit the additional evidence, and its admission of that evidence was justified in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(4) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 empowers the appellate authority to make further inquiry as it thinks fit, including by admitting additional evidence when the facts and pleadings warrant it. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K.M. Charia Abdullah & Co. for the principle that statutory power to make further inquiry supports such evidence-gathering for fair disposal of an appeal.

rule.if: rent_control_appeal and further_inquiry_authorized and evidence_warranted_for_fair_disposal and opposing_party_could_address_evidence and not unfair_prejudice

predicates.rent_control_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a rent-control authority’s decision in an eviction matter.
predicates.further_inquiry_authorized: The governing appeal process authorizes the appellate authority to make further inquiry.
predicates.evidence_warranted_for_fair_disposal: The facts and pleadings make the additional evidence relevant to fair disposal of the appeal.
predicates.opposing_party_could_address_evidence: The opposing party had an opportunity to test and make submissions about the additional evidence.
predicates.unfair_prejudice: The additional evidence caused unfair prejudice to the opposing party.

issues.definition: When a rent-control appeal authorizes further inquiry, relevant additional evidence may be admitted if the opposing party can address it and its admission causes no unfair prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate authority’s failure to cite specific portions of the first-instance decision does not by itself establish that it failed to consider the evidence recorded there.
material_facts: The appellate authority referred to the Rent Controller’s findings and considered additional evidence.
Although it did not identify specific paragraphs of the Rent Controller’s decision, its order showed awareness of the evidence led before the Controller.
issues.conclusion: The appellate authority had considered the evidence before the Rent Controller, and the tenant’s criticism on that ground was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the appellate order as a whole and held that omission of specific references to paragraphs of the first-instance decision did not show that the underlying evidence had been ignored.

predicates.rent_control_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a rent-control eviction matter.
predicates.appellate_order_addresses_first_instance: The appellate authority’s order refers to the findings made by the first-instance authority.
predicates.appellate_order_shows_awareness_of_first: The appellate order shows that the authority knew evidence had been presented before the first-instance authority.
predicates.not_specific_paragraph_citations: The appellate order does not cite particular paragraphs of the first-instance decision.

issues.definition: In a rent-control appeal, an order that addresses the first-instance findings and shows awareness of its evidence does not demonstrate non-consideration merely because it lacks specific paragraph citations.

issues.legal_issue: Property devolving on a father under statutory succession does not become Hindu joint-family property in his hands as against his own sons merely because it came from his father.
material_facts: The family was governed by the Mitakshara school of Hindu law.
The property in the ancestral house devolved on the landlord’s father on the death of the landlord’s grandfather.
The tenant argued that the landlord had a coparcenary interest in that house and therefore occupied another residential house.
issues.conclusion: The property that devolved on the landlord’s father was not Hindu joint-family property in his hands vis-à-vis his sons, and the appellate authority was right to treat the landlord as occupying the house with his father’s permission.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property inherited in the circumstances addressed in Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen is taken by the heir in his individual capacity, not as property of a Hindu undivided family vis-à-vis his own sons. The Court also considered State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram and Sundarsanam Maistri v. Narasimhulu Maistri, and held Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Rani Deoraj Kuari inapplicable.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a landlord may recover residential premises from a tenant.
predicates.property_devolved_on_parent_by_statutory: The property devolved on a parent by statutory succession from an earlier generation.
predicates.claimant_is_parent_descendant: The person claiming a family-property interest is a descendant of the parent who inherited the property.

issues.definition: When property devolves on a parent by statutory succession, a descendant’s claim that it is Hindu joint-family property against that parent is not established merely by the property’s source in an earlier generation.

issues.legal_issue: Shared family accommodation that is substantially inadequate for the landlord’s family does not defeat a finding of bona fide residential need merely because the landlord may have an interest in the accommodation.
material_facts: The family’s ancestral house had two rooms used by several brothers and their families.
Even counting a large room formerly used as a commercial bank’s chamber, the accommodation was insufficient for the landlord’s reasonable needs.
The appellate authority found the landlord’s residential requirement bona fide.
issues.conclusion: The finding of bona fide need was sustainable even if the landlord was treated as having an interest in the ancestral house and the additional room was counted as available accommodation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(3)(a)(i) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 permits recovery of a residential building for the landlord’s own occupation when the statutory requirements are met. The Court held that the shared accommodation’s inadequacy supported the bona fide-need finding regardless of whether the landlord was a licensee or a co-owner.

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction from residential premises on the ground of the landlord’s own residential need.
predicates.family_shares_existing_home: The landlord’s family shares an existing home with other family members.
predicates.available_accommodation_is_insufficient_: The accommodation available in that home is insufficient for the reasonable needs of the landlord’s family.

issues.definition: In a residential eviction proceeding, a family’s shared home supports a finding of bona fide need when its available accommodation is insufficient for the family.

issues.legal_issue: A recital that vacant possession was given does not necessarily establish that a property was physically vacant, and evidence may explain what possession the recital conveyed.
material_facts: A registered document relied on by the tenant recited that vacant possession of another house had been given.
The landlord disputed that the house had been physically vacant, and oral evidence indicated otherwise.
The appellate authority accepted evidence that the house was not physically vacant.
issues.conclusion: The recital could refer to transfer of the legal right to possession rather than actual physical possession, and oral evidence was admissible to explain it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that language in a document of this kind could refer to the legal right of possession without establishing actual physical vacant possession. It relied on Lachhman Das v. Rent Control and Eviction Officer for the permissibility of evidence explaining the recital.

rule.if: residential_eviction_proceeding and deed_recites_vacant_possession and physical_vacancy_is_disputed and explanatory_evidence_is_offered

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction from residential premises and the landlord’s availability of another house.
predicates.deed_recites_vacant_possession: A document states that vacant possession of another property was given.
predicates.physical_vacancy_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether the property was actually physically vacant.
predicates.explanatory_evidence_is_offered: A party offers evidence to explain the meaning or practical effect of the document’s possession recital.

issues.definition: When a possession recital is disputed as proof of physical vacancy, evidence may establish that it conveyed a legal right to possession without actual physical vacancy.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord is not disqualified from seeking eviction merely because the landlord purchased and sold another house before filing the eviction petition when that house was not physically vacant and there is no evidence that the sale was intended to defeat the tenant’s claim.
material_facts: The landlord purchased another house and later sold it before instituting the eviction proceeding.
The appellate authority found that the landlord had not obtained physical vacant possession of that house and rejected the allegation that the sale was benami.
There was no evidence that the sale was made to defeat the tenant’s claim or evade the statutory restriction.
issues.conclusion: The prior purchase and sale did not establish that the landlord occupied another residential building or otherwise disqualify the landlord from seeking eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(3)(a)(i) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 sets out conditions concerning the landlord’s occupation of another residential building and prior vacation of such a building. The Court held that the Act must be read reasonably and justly, consistently with the presumption of constitutionality, and not to impose an unwarranted restriction on property rights. It relied on State of Karnataka v. Hans Corporation, K.P. Varghese v. Income Tax Officer, and Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir.

rule.if: residential_eviction_proceeding and other_house_sold_before_petition and other_house_not_physically_vacant and not evidence_sale_intended_to_defeat_tenant_claim

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is an eviction claim based on the landlord’s own residential need.
predicates.other_house_sold_before_petition: The landlord sold another house before instituting the eviction proceeding.
predicates.other_house_not_physically_vacant: The landlord had not obtained physical vacant possession of the other house.
predicates.evidence_sale_intended_to_defeat_tenant_: Evidence shows that the sale was intended to defeat the tenant’s claim or evade a statutory restriction.

issues.definition: A landlord’s pre-petition sale of another house does not disqualify the landlord when the house was not physically vacant and the sale was not shown to be intended to defeat the tenant’s claim.
